title: How to Calculate Prorated Rent for a Mid-Month Move-In or Move-Out
meta: Prorated rent three ways: actual days, a 30-day month or a 365-day year, with $1,800 rent and an 18th move-in worked out for 30- and 31-day months.
html:
Prorated rent is your monthly rent turned into a daily rate and multiplied by the days you actually live in the unit. With $1,800 rent and a move-in on the 18th of a 30-day month, you owe for 13 days, which comes to $780 under the most common method. Landlords use three different ways to set that daily rate, though, and in some months the answers differ by more than $50.

The three methods, step by step

  1. Count the days you will occupy the unit. Most leases count move-in day, because you have the keys that day. Moving in on the 18th of a 30-day month covers the 18th through the 30th, which is 13 days. In a 31-day month it is 14 days.
  2. Find the daily rate using the method your lease names.
    • Actual days in the month. Divide the rent by the number of days in that specific month: $1,800 / 30 = $60.00, $1,800 / 31 = $58.06, and $1,800 / 28 = $64.29 in a non-leap February.
    • 30-day month. Divide the rent by 30 no matter what the calendar says, so the daily rate is always $60.00. This is sometimes called a banker's month.
    • 365-day year. Multiply the rent by 12 and divide by 365: $21,600 / 365 = $59.18 a day, the same in every month.
  3. Multiply the daily rate by the number of days. Round the final amount, not the daily rate, if you want your figure to match the landlord's spreadsheet to the cent.

Worked example: $1,800 rent, moving in on the 18th

Here is the same move-in date run through all three methods in a 30-day month (such as September) and a 31-day month (such as October).

Method30-day month: daily rate30-day month: 13 days owed31-day month: daily rate31-day month: 14 days owed
Actual days in the month$60.00$780.00$58.06$812.90
30-day month$60.00$780.00$60.00$840.00
365-day year$59.18$769.32$59.18$828.49

In a 30-day month, two methods agree on $780 and the yearly method comes in about $11 lower. In a 31-day month the spread widens: the 30-day convention charges $840, which is $27.10 more than the actual-days method, because it prices the 31st at a full $60. If your lease uses the 30-day convention, ask whether the 31st is billed at all. A landlord who treats every month as 30 days may charge 13 days ($780) rather than 14.

Rounding also explains small gaps. Rounding the daily rate first gives $58.06 x 14 = $812.84, six cents less than the $812.90 you get from the unrounded rate. Gaps of tens of dollars usually mean a different method or day count.

February magnifies the differences. A move-in on February 18 of a 28-day February is 11 days: $707.14 by actual days, $660.00 by a 30-day month and $650.96 by a 365-day year. In a leap year February has 29 days, so recount before you pay. When a partial stay spans two months, a date calculator that counts the days between two dates helps you avoid off-by-one mistakes; just decide first whether the end date counts.

What to check in the lease before you pay

  • Whether the first month is prorated at all. Some landlords prorate the move-in month; others charge a full first month and prorate the second, or simply start the lease on the 1st. Rules vary by state and city, so the lease and local law control.
  • Which daily-rate method applies. Look for words like "per diem," "daily rate," "30-day month" or "365 days." If the lease is silent, ask for the method in writing before you sign.
  • Whether move-in day counts. One day at $60 is real money.
  • When the prorated amount is due. Many landlords collect it together with the first full month. In the example above, that means $780 plus $1,800, or $2,580, before you get the keys, plus any security deposit.
  • Which other charges follow the same rule. Flat fees for parking, pets or utilities may or may not be prorated. The security deposit is not rent and is normally not prorated.

Prorating the last month when you move out

Move-out proration uses the same arithmetic in reverse, but it is less often automatic. Many fixed-term leases end on the last day of a month, and leaving early can mean owing the full month. Where your lease or a month-to-month agreement allows a mid-month end date, you pay only for the days you keep the unit.

Say your tenancy ends on the 10th and the rent is still $1,800. In a 30-day month you would owe $600 under either the actual-days or the 30-day method, or $591.78 under the 365-day method. In a 31-day month the actual-days method drops to $580.65, while the 30-day method stays at $600.

Notice rules matter as much as the math. Month-to-month agreements commonly require written notice, often 30 days, but the required period depends on your state and your agreement. A days-from-today calculator shows which date falls 30 or 60 days from the day you hand in notice, so you can see whether your planned move-out date works.

Prorated rent questions renters ask

Is move-in day counted?
Usually yes, since you can use the unit that day. Some landlords start billing the day after a late-evening key handoff, so confirm the start date on the lease or move-in sheet.

Which method is the fairest?
The actual-days method matches the calendar exactly, and the 365-day method gives a steady daily rate that adds up to exactly 12 months of rent over a 365-day year (one day more in a leap year). The 30-day method charges more than the calendar in 31-day months and less in February.

My landlord's number is higher than mine. What should I do?
Ask which method and which dates were used, and request the calculation in writing. If you still disagree, your state or local housing agency can explain the rules where you live; HUD's website points renters to tenant-rights information and rental help by state.

Try it with your numbers: count your billable days with the Date Calculator, then multiply by the daily rate your lease uses.

Sources

  • U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)
  • U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications (calendars and dates)

All amounts were computed in Python from $1,800 rent and the stated dates, rounding only the final dollar figure. Last reviewed: November 2026. This is general information, not legal advice; your lease and your state or local landlord-tenant law decide what you actually owe.

title: Biweekly Mortgage Payments: What You Actually Save on a $300,000 Loan
meta: On a $300,000 loan at 6.5%, biweekly payments cut 5 years 8 months and about $84,000 of interest. Compare it with adding 1/12 extra every month.
html:
Paying half your mortgage payment every two weeks adds up to 26 half-payments a year, which equals 13 full monthly payments instead of 12. On a $300,000, 30-year fixed loan at 6.5%, that one extra payment a year pays the loan off about 5 years and 8 months early and saves roughly $84,000 in interest. You can get nearly the same result, with no special program, by adding one-twelfth of a payment to every monthly bill.

Where the extra payment comes from

A year has 52 weeks, so paying every two weeks means 26 payments. The monthly principal-and-interest payment on $300,000 at 6.5% for 30 years is $1,896.20, and half of that is $948.10.

  • 12 monthly payments: 12 x $1,896.20 = $22,754.40 a year
  • 26 half-payments: 26 x $948.10 = $24,650.60 a year
  • Difference: $1,896.20, exactly one extra monthly payment

That extra payment is the whole trick. Because your scheduled payment already covers the month's interest, every extra dollar that reaches the loan goes straight to principal, and a lower principal means less interest every month after that. These figures cover principal and interest only; property taxes and homeowners insurance held in escrow are separate. To see your full monthly cost with taxes, insurance and PMI, run your loan through the mortgage calculator.

Side by side: $300,000 at 6.5% for 30 years

The table comes from a month-by-month amortization: each month, interest is charged at 6.5% / 12 on the remaining balance and the payment is subtracted. The biweekly row assumes the extra payment is applied to principal once a year, which is how many programs that collect half-payments and forward them monthly end up working. The last row adds $158.02, one-twelfth of a payment, to each monthly bill.

StrategyWhat you payExtra per yearPayoff timeTotal interestInterest saved
Standard monthly$1,896.20 a month$030 years (360 payments)$382,633None
Biweekly (extra applied once a year)$948.10 every two weeks$1,896.2024 years 4 months$298,649$83,985
Monthly plus 1/12 extra$2,054.22 a month$1,896.2024 years 2 months$295,377$87,256

Both strategies put the same $1,896.20 a year toward the loan. The 1/12 approach comes out slightly ahead because the extra money reaches principal a little sooner each month instead of in one lump at the end of the year. If your servicer credits each half-payment to the loan the day it arrives, a true biweekly schedule lands close to the 1/12 row. The gap between any of these and doing nothing is far larger than the gap between them.

The catch with third-party biweekly programs

Biweekly plans are sold by some servicers and by outside payment companies, and the details vary widely. Before enrolling, look for these problems:

  • Fees. Some programs charge an enrollment fee, a fee on every debit, or both. A hypothetical $2.50 per debit is $65 a year (26 x $2.50) for something you can do yourself for free.
  • Money that sits. Some programs hold your half-payments and send one full payment a month. Your money waits in their account, and the extra payment is only sent once a year.
  • Extra money that is not applied to principal. If the extra amount is held as an unapplied payment or credited toward a future payment, it does not reduce your balance early and saves little or nothing.

If a program cannot show you, in writing, when each payment is credited and how the extra goes to principal, skip it.

How to do it yourself, free

  1. Check for a prepayment penalty. Look at the Loan Terms section of your Closing Disclosure or ask your servicer. Many loans have none, but confirm before you start.
  2. Ask how extra payments are applied. Tell your servicer, in writing or through the online portal, that any amount above the scheduled payment should go to principal. Many portals have a separate principal-only field.
  3. Pick a method. Add $158.02 to each monthly payment, send one extra payment a year (a tax refund works), or use a free biweekly option from your servicer if it credits payments promptly.
  4. Verify on your statement. The principal balance should drop by the extra amount the month you send it. If it does not, call the servicer and ask where the money went.

To see how each extra dollar changes your own payoff date, a loan calculator with an amortization schedule lets you compare the standard schedule with a higher payment.

Questions before you switch to biweekly

Will paying biweekly lower my monthly payment?
No. On a fixed-rate loan, extra principal shortens the loan but the required payment stays the same. Some lenders offer a recast, which re-figures the payment after a large lump sum, usually for a fee.

Is the extra payment better than keeping the cash?
It depends on your situation. Many people first build an emergency fund and pay off high-interest debt, because money sent to a mortgage is hard to get back without borrowing or selling the home.

Does this work if my rate is lower than 6.5%?
Yes, an extra payment always shortens a loan, but the dollars saved are smaller at a lower rate. The 6.5% here is an illustration; Freddie Mac publishes weekly averages if you want a current benchmark.

Can I stop at any time?
If you prepay on your own, yes: just go back to the regular payment. A third-party program may have its own cancellation terms, so read them first.

Try it with your numbers: put your balance, rate and remaining term into the Loan Calculator, then rerun it with your payment plus one-twelfth.

Sources

  • Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Mortgages
  • CFPB: Buying a house (Owning a Home)
  • Freddie Mac: Primary Mortgage Market Survey (weekly average rates)

Payoff times and interest totals come from a month-by-month Python amortization at 6.5% / 12, principal and interest only, rounded to the dollar. Last reviewed: November 2026. This is general information, not financial advice; your loan terms and your servicer's crediting rules determine what you actually save.

title: How Long Does It Take to Save $10,000? Timelines by Monthly Amount
meta: Saving $500 a month reaches $10,000 in 20 months and $300 takes 34. Compare timelines at 0% and 4% APY, with and without a $1,000 head start.
html:
Saving $500 a month gets you to $10,000 in 20 months; $300 a month takes 34 months, and $800 a month takes 13. Earning 4% APY in a high-yield savings account trims a couple of months off the slowest plan but barely moves the faster ones, because your deposits do most of the work. A $1,000 head start shortens every timeline more than the interest does.

The timeline table

Assumptions: you deposit at the end of each month, 4% APY is converted to its equivalent monthly rate (about 0.327% a month), and the goal counts as reached the first month the balance is $10,000 or more.

Monthly depositStarting balanceMonths at 0%Months at 4% APYInterest earned by then (4% APY)
$300$03432$503
$500$02020$317
$800$01313$207
$300$1,0003029$510
$500$1,0001818$315
$800$1,0001212$215

Read the table by rows first. The monthly deposit sets the pace: going from $300 to $500 cuts 14 months, and from $500 to $800 cuts another 7. Then read across: interest only changes the finish line when the plan is long. At $800 a month you are done in about a year, and the roughly $200 of interest is a pleasant bonus rather than a strategy.

The head start rows show why a tax refund or a bonus is worth parking in savings. At $300 a month, $1,000 up front saves 4 months at 0%, compared with the 2 months that 4% APY saves on its own. To test other deposits, rates or starting balances, the compound interest calculator runs the same math with monthly deposits.

Three common beliefs about savings rates, checked

"I should wait until I find the best rate."

Not true over a short horizon. At $500 a month, 4% APY earns $317 over 20 months, about 3% of the goal. Starting this month matters more than shopping for an extra fraction of a percent. You can move the money later.

"The rate doesn't matter on small balances."

Partly true, but it adds up on slow plans. On the 34-month $300 plan, 4% APY adds $503, close to two months of deposits. At $100 a month the gap is bigger: about 100 months at 0% versus 87 months at 4% APY.

"A 4% APY is locked in once I open the account."

No. Savings account rates are variable and can change at any time, often following moves in the Federal Reserve's policy rate. Treat 4% as an example, not a promise, and check your bank's current APY.

How $10,000 fits into an emergency fund

A common guideline is to keep three to six months of essential expenses in an emergency fund. If your rent or mortgage, groceries, utilities, insurance, transportation and minimum debt payments add up to $3,000 a month, $10,000 covers a little over three months. If your essentials run $5,000 a month, it covers two.

  • Keep it separate. A dedicated savings account makes it less likely the money drifts into everyday spending.
  • Keep it reachable. An emergency fund needs to be available within a day or two, which is why savings and money market deposit accounts are typical homes for it.
  • Revisit the target. Prices change over time; an inflation calculator shows how much more the same monthly expenses may cost in a few years.
  • Automate it. A transfer scheduled for the day after payday is the simplest way to stay on the table's timeline.

Make sure the money is insured

Deposits at an FDIC-insured bank are covered up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category, so a $10,000 savings goal is well within the limit. Two things are worth checking:

  • Is it actually a bank? Some savings apps are not banks and place your money at a partner bank. FDIC insurance protects you if an insured bank fails, not if the app company itself fails. The FDIC's BankFind tool lets you confirm a bank's insurance.
  • Credit unions that are federally insured are covered separately by the National Credit Union Administration, with the same $250,000 standard amount. Check that yours is federally insured.

Interest is taxable income. Banks generally send a Form 1099-INT if you earn $10 or more in interest during the year, so the roughly $200 to $510 of interest in the table belongs on your tax return.

Questions savers ask about a $10,000 goal

Should I pay off credit card debt first?
Card interest rates are usually far higher than savings rates, so many people keep a small starter cushion, then send extra money to the card, and then return to the $10,000 goal.

What if I can only save $100 a month?
It still works, just slowly: about 100 months at 0% or 87 months at 4% APY. Adding windfalls such as refunds or gifts shortens that quickly.

Is a CD better than a savings account?
A certificate of deposit can lock in a rate, which helps if rates fall, but early withdrawal usually costs a penalty. For emergency money, many savers keep at least part in a regular savings account.

Try it with your numbers: enter your starting balance, monthly deposit and current APY in the Compound Interest Calculator to see the month you cross $10,000.

Sources

  • FDIC: deposit insurance
  • Investor.gov (SEC): Compound Interest Calculator
  • MyMoney.gov: federal financial literacy resources

Every timeline was simulated month by month in Python with end-of-month deposits and 4% APY converted to an equivalent monthly rate. Last reviewed: November 2026. This is general information, not financial advice; savings rates change often, so check your bank's current APY and terms.

title: Oven Temperature Conversion: Celsius, Fahrenheit and Gas Mark Chart
meta: Gas mark 4 is 350°F or about 180°C. See the full chart from gas mark 1/4 to 9, the °C/°F formula and the fan oven rule of 25°F or 20°C lower.
html:
Gas mark 4, 350°F and 180°C are the same moderate oven setting, and the chart below lists every step from gas mark 1/4 to gas mark 9. For any other number, use °C = (°F - 32) x 5/9, or °F = °C x 9/5 + 32. If you bake in a convection or fan oven, start about 25°F or 20°C lower than a recipe written for a conventional oven.

Oven temperature chart: gas mark, °F and °C

The "exact °C" column is the formula result. The "recipe °C" column shows the rounded values you will see in most British and European recipes, and the fan column subtracts 20°C from that.

Gas mark°FExact °CRecipe °CFan oven °CDescription
1/4225107.211090Very cool
1/2250121.1120100Very cool
1275135.0140120Cool
2300148.9150130Cool
3325162.8160 to 170140 to 150Warm
4350176.7180160Moderate
5375190.6190170Moderately hot
6400204.4200180Hot
7425218.3220200Hot
8450232.2230210Very hot
9475246.1240220Very hot

Gas marks are mainly used in the UK and Ireland. Each step on the chart is 25°F, which is why the Fahrenheit column climbs so neatly while the Celsius values need rounding.

The formula, with two worked conversions

  1. Fahrenheit to Celsius: subtract 32, then multiply by 5/9. For 350°F: 350 - 32 = 318, and 318 x 5/9 = 176.7°C. Recipes round this to 180°C.
  2. Celsius to Fahrenheit: multiply by 9/5, then add 32. For 200°C: 200 x 9/5 = 360, and 360 + 32 = 392°F. Set a U.S. oven to 400°F.

Skip the "double it and add 30" shortcut that works for weather. At oven heat it overshoots badly: it turns 180°C into 390°F when the real answer is 356°F, and 200°C into 430°F instead of 392°F.

One more detail: a temperature difference converts without the 32. A 25°F drop is about 14°C, and a 20°C drop is 36°F. So the two common versions of the fan-oven rule are not identical; both are rounded starting points, not precise conversions.

Why recipes round, and when it matters

  • Oven dials use steps. Many U.S. dials move in 25°F steps and many European ones in 10°C steps, so 176.7°C has to become 180°C anyway.
  • Ovens swing. Most home ovens cycle the heat on and off, so the air temperature drifts above and below the setting. A few degrees of rounding is usually smaller than that swing.
  • Delicate bakes are the exception. Meringues, custards and some cookies are sensitive to small differences. For those, use the exact conversion, check early and trust visual cues.

Convection and fan ovens

A fan moves hot air around the food, so it cooks and browns faster at the same setting. The usual adjustment is to lower the temperature about 25°F (or 20°C) and start checking for doneness a little before the recipe's time. Two cautions:

  • Don't subtract twice. British recipes often print both, as in "180°C (160°C fan)." Use the fan number as written. Many newer ovens also have an automatic convection conversion setting that lowers the temperature for you, so check the manual.
  • Air fryers work like small convection ovens. If you adapt a conventional oven recipe, the same reduction is a reasonable starting point; check the food early.

Check your oven with a thermometer

  1. Hang an inexpensive oven thermometer from the center of the middle rack.
  2. Preheat to 350°F (180°C) and wait 15 to 20 minutes after the preheat signal.
  3. Take two or three readings about 10 minutes apart and average them, since the thermostat cycles.
  4. If the average is 325°F when the dial says 350°F, set the dial 25°F higher, or follow the manual to recalibrate.

Converting a recipe from another country usually means converting more than heat. Recipes that use Celsius tend to weigh flour and sugar in grams, which a grams to cups converter translates into U.S. cups, and list liquids in milliliters, which an ml to oz converter turns into fluid ounces.

Oven temperature questions from the kitchen

What is 180°C in Fahrenheit?
Exactly 356°F. Set a U.S. oven to 350°F, the standard equivalent.

What temperature is gas mark 6?
400°F, or 200°C in a conventional oven and about 180°C in a fan oven.

My recipe says 425°F but my oven is Celsius only. What do I use?
425°F is 218.3°C, so set 220°C, or about 200°C if the oven is fan-assisted.

Why does my food burn even when I follow the chart?
The oven may run hot, the pan may sit too close to the heating element, or a dark pan may brown faster. An oven thermometer tells you which problem you have.

Try it with your numbers: once the temperature is sorted, convert the ingredient weights with the Grams to Cups Converter.

Sources

  • NIST: SI units (including temperature and the degree Celsius)
  • NIST Office of Weights and Measures: metric and unit conversions

Every Celsius value was computed in Python from the exact formula and compared with the rounded figures common in UK and European recipes. Last reviewed: November 2026. This is general kitchen guidance; ovens vary, so follow your appliance manual and check food for doneness.
